documents.title: Academic Integrity Policy (file name 2011-03; includes AI language)
documents.summary: Seattle University's registrar-hosted Academic Integrity Policy is an all-purpose integrity policy that names generative AI in its plagiarism definition and a cheating example, leaves AI prohibitions to faculty, and sets the reporting, appeal and sanction process used for AI cases. It does not give students a list of allowed uses.
documents.stance_why: The policy says 'Faculty members are permitted to have specific policies regarding the use of AI programs, including prohibiting their use' and treats AI output as cheating only 'if prohibited by the faculty member', so it sets no university-wide ban or permission and hands the decision to instructors, apart from requiring citation of AI output.

units.why: The definition names 'the outputs of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs' presented as one's own without citation as plagiarism, so uncited AI output becomes an integrity offense; classed P36 (misconduct) rather than P24 because it defines the violation, with the citation duty in the next unit.
units.anchor: outputs of Generative Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) programs when presented as one’s own work

units.fit_note: Also says intent is irrelevant: undisclosed AI output is plagiarism 'regardless of intent'.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on actor, phase, modality and type (P36) but A set unit_stance restrict and B prohibit. The definition makes AI output plagiarism only when 'presented as one's own work without appropriate citation', so cited AI use is not banned; restrict is the closer reading.

units.why: Students are told they 'are responsible for educating themselves as to the proper mode of attributing credit in any course or field', which applies to AI output because the plagiarism definition covers it; P78 fits (students learn each course's rules).

Kept as a real policy statement though it is not AI-specific (A's fit_note).

units.why: Examples of plagiarism include code or papers from 'AI program’s output without proper citation and/or acknowledgment, as required by faculty', so students must cite or acknowledge AI output where faculty require it; P24 fits because the rule is about citation/acknowledgment.

documents.title: Guidelines for AI Use in Teaching and Research
documents.summary: A faculty-focused guideline from the Technology Ethics Initiative, adopted by the Academic Technology Committee, setting out principles for AI in teaching (educational benefit, academic integrity, data privacy) and in research. It declines a blanket rule and tells instructors to set course-specific policies, state them in syllabi, ask for acknowledgment of AI use, and not rely on detectors.

documents.summary: The Center for Faculty Development's syllabus template includes a generative AI section (added 2025-08-11) with guidance and three sample statements: not permitted, limited, and permitted. It asks instructors to state a policy and rationale and leaves the choice to them; the AI section is not marked as required.

notes: Reconciled from coder A and B. Only the three included university-layer documents were coded; no school, computing or course documents were collected. Process and sanction units in the academic integrity policy apply to all integrity violations, not only AI. The syllabus template's AI section is optional guidance (not marked required); repeated sample sentences in samples 2 and 3 are coded once. Neither coder proposed new types; one unit (hallucination-minimizing tool selection) is UNCOVERED.
